idiom_name: TcpListener/TcpClient role split; Kestrel connection middleware
implementation_notes: The BCL separates the roles: TcpListener.Start() + AcceptTcpClientAsync(CancellationToken) accepts; TcpClient.ConnectAsync(...) dials; both yield connected endpoints handed to a per-connection handler. ASP.NET Core internalises the accept loop in Kestrel and exposes only the handler/middleware layer. Use TcpListener.Pending() to check the queue without blocking before calling AcceptTcpClientAsync; dispose TcpClient/listener deterministically to avoid descriptor recycling. For high throughput, prefer SocketsHttpHandler with connection pooling over raw TcpClient.
pitfalls: Cancelling a pending accept needs the CancellationToken overload; plainly calling Stop() surfaces an exception.
Unbounded accept loops exhaust sockets or threads; bound the concurrency with a SemaphoreSlim.
Dispose TcpClient/listener deterministically so descriptors are not recycled late.
TcpClient shares the underlying Socket; calling Close() on one affects the other.
SocketsHttpHandler is the preferred HttpClient factory for connection pooling; managing raw TcpClient per request wastes connections.
